title: Avatar to Avengers: The Highest-Grossing Hollywood Films at India's Box Office
excerpt: Avatar: The Way of Water tops the all-time list at ₹390.6 crore, with 21 Hollywood films now in India's ₹100 crore club as the market accelerates.
body:
• Avatar: The Way of Water leads all Hollywood films in India with ₹390.6 crore net, followed by Avengers: Endgame at ₹373.22 crore.
  • Marvel and Disney dominate the top 10, holding seven of the ten spots, while the Avatar franchise claims three entries across the full list.
  • Six films released in 2025-2026 have already entered the all-time top 30, reflecting India's accelerating appetite for Hollywood tentpoles.
  • The ₹100 crore threshold — once rare for Hollywood films in India — has now been crossed by 21 titles, with four added in 2025 alone.

Avatar and the Avengers Rule India

James Cameron's Avatar: The Way of Water holds the top position on the all-time list of highest-grossing Hollywood films at the Indian box office, with a net collection of ₹390.6 crore since its December 2022 release. The sequel outpaced Avengers: Endgame (₹373.22 crore), which had held the crown since 2019.

The top five is rounded out by Avengers: Infinity War (₹227.43 crore), Spider-Man: No Way Home (₹212 crore), and Avatar: Fire and Ash (₹190.5 crore) — the third Avatar instalment, released in 2025. The original Avatar, released in 2009, sits at eighth position with ₹141.25 crore, giving the franchise three entries in the top 10.

Marvel's Stranglehold on Indian Screens

The Marvel Cinematic Universe dominates the rankings like no other franchise. Seven of the top 12 spots belong to Marvel films, from Endgame and Infinity War at the top to Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness at ₹126.94 crore. The MCU's grip extends deep into the list — Spider-Man: Far From Home (₹85.7 crore), Captain Marvel (₹84.2 crore), and Thor: Love and Thunder (₹101.45 crore) all sit comfortably in the top 25.

Disney's live-action remakes have carved their own niche. The Jungle Book, released in 2016, remains the sixth-highest Hollywood grosser in India at ₹188 crore — a figure that reflects both the film's quality and the deep cultural connection Indian audiences have with Rudyard Kipling's stories, set in Indian forests. The Lion King (₹150.09 crore) and Mufasa: The Lion King (₹135.35 crore) further cement Disney's strength.

The ₹100 Crore Club Expands

Crossing ₹100 crore net at the Indian box office was once an extraordinary feat for a Hollywood film. As of July 2026, 21 titles have achieved it. The pace is accelerating: four films crossed the threshold in 2025 alone — Avatar: Fire and Ash, Mission: Impossible – The Final Reckoning (₹106.9 crore), F1 (₹102.82 crore), and Jurassic World Rebirth (₹100.56 crore).

The 2026 entries on the list already include Obsession (₹84.65 crore), Project Hail Mary (₹75.21 crore), Michael (₹70.76 crore), and The Odyssey (₹56.66 crore), with several still in theatrical runs.

Action Franchises and the Franchise Effect

The data reveals India's clear preference for franchise-driven spectacle. The Fast & Furious series places four films in the top 50, led by Furious 7 at ₹110 crore. The Mission: Impossible franchise has three entries, with Dead Reckoning Part One (₹120 crore) the highest. The Jurassic World trilogy collectively grossed over ₹273 crore across its three instalments.

Standalone films occasionally break through — Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer earned ₹129 crore in 2023, and Joker collected ₹64 crore in 2019 — but they remain exceptions. The Conjuring horror franchise, with three films on the list totalling nearly ₹189 crore, shows that even mid-budget genre films can find a massive Indian audience when marketed as event releases.

India's Growing Weight in Hollywood's Global Calculus

India is now among the top five international markets for Hollywood tentpoles. Studios increasingly plan India-specific release strategies, Hindi and regional language dubbing, and marketing campaigns tailored to Indian audiences. For the diaspora, the list reflects a cultural crossover that runs both ways — Indian audiences embracing global pop culture while Hollywood increasingly courts the subcontinent as an essential revenue stream.
